props.detent: Overshoot as the mechanism seats. 0 arrives dead, which reads as software; a little bounce reads as a part with mass hitting its stop.
props.bladeCurvature: Curvature of each blade's inner edge. The mechanism is derived from the opening range, so this bends the leaf without touching the travel: flatter blades cut a rounder, more regular polygon, tighter ones pull the scallop corners out into a star.
props.edgeHighlight: Strength of the seam along each leaf's inner edge, and of the bezel. Each seam is cut by the leaf that lies over it — named rather than left to the drawing order, because a leaf stack is a ring and painter's order is a line. That is what puts exactly one line at every corner of the opening, wide open and shut alike.
props.housingInset: Width of the machined ring inside the rim. It is drawn over the blades, so the housing reads as the part they are seated in rather than one more leaf.
props.autoOpen: Open and shut on a loop. Turning it off hands the mechanism to the openness slider.
props.bladeColor: Body of the blades, the housing, and the barrel floor behind them. Its own material rather than a themed surface — a light theme must not put a white ring around a lens.
props.edgeColor: Amethyst on the blade seams and the bezel.

segmented.description: A segmented control whose indicator travels on a shared layout id and smears in the direction it is moving.

props.indicator: How the active segment is marked. All three are the same travelling element at different settings — the shared layout id does not change, so switching between them costs no extra animation code.
props.sizing: Auto sizes each segment to its label, so the indicator resizes as well as travels — the half of the FLIP that equal-width tabs never show. Equal splits the row evenly and fills the container.
props.density: Padding and type size. Compact is the toolbar setting; it shortens the travel too, which is why the smear reads more subtly there.
props.radius: Corner radius of the indicator and the segments. motion corrects the radius through the layout animation, so a rounded indicator does not go oval while it is resizing.
props.stiffness: Spring tension on the travel. It also drives the proxy spring the deformation is read from, so the smear stays in phase with the movement at every setting rather than at the one it was tuned on.
props.damping: Spring friction. Low lets the indicator ring past the segment and come back, which the smear follows in both directions; high arrives dead and barely deforms at all.
props.smear: How hard the travel deforms the indicator. The stretch is along the direction of movement and anchored at the leading edge, so it trails behind rather than running ahead. Zero is a rigid box that slides.
props.glow: Accent bloom under the indicator. It travels with the box and takes the same deformation, so it reads as light coming off the thing rather than a separate shape following it.
props.accentColor: The indicator, its bloom, and the label of the active segment when the indicator is not filling it.

tether.description: A popover that grows out of the corner nearest its trigger, and moves that origin when it flips.

props.side: Preferred side. The transform origin is derived from the side the panel actually resolved to, never this one — a flip that keeps the requested origin grows the panel away from the trigger it just moved to.
props.align: Where the panel sits along that side. It moves the origin and the caret together, so a start-aligned panel below the trigger grows down and to the right out of the button's left corner.
props.offset: Gap between trigger and panel. Padding rather than margin: a pointer crossing the gap on its way into a hover-opened panel never leaves the component, so the panel does not close under the cursor.
props.stiffness: Spring tension on the pop. High enough to feel like the panel is already there by the time the eye arrives.
props.damping: Spring friction. A little overshoot is the pop; too little and the panel wobbles, which on a menu reads as unresponsive rather than lively.
props.popScale: Size the panel grows from. At 1 the origin work is invisible and the entrance is a plain fade — worth setting once to see what the rest of the component is buying.
props.arrow: Caret on the tethered edge. It sits where the panel is anchored, so it stays pointing at the trigger through a side change without any repositioning code.
props.flip: Move to the opposite side when the preferred one would overflow the viewport. The fit test reads the panel's layout box rather than its bounding rect, because the rect carries the entrance scale and would decide using a box smaller than the one about to be there.
props.openOn: What opens the panel. Click also moves focus into it; hover deliberately does not, and answers focus on the trigger instead so the keyboard is not locked out of a pointer-only affordance.
props.closeDelay: Grace period before a hover-opened panel closes. The timer also refuses to fire while focus is still inside, so a pointer wandering off cannot destroy the element someone is tabbing through.
props.radius: Panel corner radius.
props.accentColor: The rule on the tethered edge and the caret. Both move with a flip, so the panel keeps pointing back at its origin on whichever side it ended up.

inline-edit.description: Text that becomes its own input with nothing moving. One padded box, two contents, sized in CSS.

props.commitOn: Blur commits when focus leaves. Explicit grows a confirm and a cancel outside the box and treats losing focus as a cancel. Both are defensible, which is why it is a prop rather than a decision.
props.stiffness: Spring tension on the border, wash and ring arriving. This is the only thing that animates — everything else is already exactly where it will be.
props.damping: Spring friction on the same. Low overshoots the colour, which on a border reads as a flash rather than as bounce.
props.underline: How the display state says it is editable. A text decoration rather than a border, because a border would have to be reserved in the editing state too — and none is the honest option for a row that already announces itself some other way.
props.padX: Horizontal padding. Shared by both states by construction: it lives on the shell, which never unmounts, so the two contents cannot disagree about it.
props.padY: Vertical padding. The one that shifts every row below it when an inline editor gets this wrong.
props.radius: Corner radius of the shell.
props.selectOnEdit: Select the whole value on entering edit, so typing replaces it. Off puts the caret where the click landed, which is the right behaviour for a long value being amended rather than renamed.
props.allowEmpty: Accept an empty commit. Off puts the previous value back, on the grounds that a blank field is a mis-click far more often than an intention.
props.showPencil: Pencil on hover and keyboard focus. Absolutely positioned outside the shell — anything rendered inside it changes the width of the box the component exists to hold still.
props.multiline: A textarea that grows by line instead of a single-line field. The growth is the same CSS trick either way: an invisible copy of the draft sized in the same grid cell, so nothing is measured in JavaScript.
props.accentColor: The border, wash and ring of the editing state, and the underline of the display state. Expected as a 6-digit hex: the transparent variants are built by suffix so the fade runs on one interpolation rather than between two colours.

crossing.description: A gallery-to-detail crossing on the View Transitions API, where one element is the same object in both views.

props.duration: Length of the crossing. Applied to the shared elements and the view together through pseudo-element rules the component scopes to itself, so it never retimes a transition something else on the page is running.
props.easing: Curve on the travel. Expressive arrives fast and settles; standard is the material curve; linear is there to show what the easing is worth, which on a morph is most of it.
props.shareTitle: Carry the title across as a second shared element. Off, only the tile travels and the title cross-fades with the rest — the clearest way to see what a shared element buys over a crossfade.
props.exit: What the outgoing copy of the tile does while the incoming one arrives. Hold keeps it opaque underneath and is the default: it is the only one with no instant where two gradients are both half there. Fade is the browser's own behaviour, kept so the difference is visible; slide sends the old one off as the new lands.
props.radius: Corner radius of the frame and, three px in, the tiles.
props.viewTransition: Run the API at all. Off takes exactly the path an unsupported browser takes — the state update, bare — which is the only honest way to see the fallback. A view transition cannot be shortened, only skipped.
props.announce: Announce the destination in a live region. A view transition is invisible to assistive tech, so a crossing that says nothing is a dead end for anyone not watching the pixels.
props.accentColor: Focus ring, and the mark on the card you came back from — drawn only once the crossing has finished. Anything painted on the shared element while it is in flight is captured into the snapshot and travels across the frame with it.

reorder.description: A sortable list that answers to a finger and to a keyboard equally. Grab a row, and the rest step aside to make the space.

props.axis: Which way the list runs, and which arrow keys move a row.
props.stiffness: Spring tension as the displaced rows close up. This is the only motion in the component that is not under your finger, so it is the one that decides whether the list feels attached to the drag.
props.damping: Spring friction on the same.
props.handle: Restrict the drag to the grip. Off makes the whole row the surface, which is quicker to hit and costs you text selection and a scroll gesture that starts on a row.
props.lift: Scale of a row while it is off the ground. Past about 1.06 the row stops reading as lifted and starts reading as a different row.
props.liftShadow: Shadow cast under a lifted row.
props.radius: Row corner radius.
props.showIndex: Print the position of each row. Worth leaving on wherever the order is the data rather than a preference — it is the only on-screen confirmation that a keyboard move landed where the announcement said it did.
props.accentColor: Grip tint, and the outline on a row the keyboard is carrying. A pointer drag shows itself by moving; a keyboard grab has to be drawn.

holofoil.description: Holographic trading-card foil over real content. The diffraction band travels against the tilt while the specular follows it, and the flake only lights where the rainbow currently falls, which is what stops the whole thing reading as one gradient sliding around.

props.maxTilt: Maximum lean at the card's edge. The tilt is only the carrier here — set it to zero and the foil still moves, because the bands are driven by pointer position rather than by the rotation.
props.perspective: Depth of the projection. Lower exaggerates the lean; the value that reads as expensive is nearly always further away than instinct suggests.
props.foil: Which diffraction pattern the laminate carries. Rainbow is the repeating twelve-stop spectrum a real holographic sheet produces — it repeats rather than running one rainbow across the card. Reverse runs it the other way so the band travels against the tilt, which is what most people actually recognise as foil.
props.foilIntensity: Strength of the diffraction band. Past about one it stops being laminate and starts being a sticker.
props.sparkle: Density of the flake. It is masked by the diffraction band rather than laid over the card, and that coupling is the entire reason the specks read as suspended inside the laminate instead of as dust on your screen.
props.glare: The broad specular band, kept separate from the foil on purpose. Foil is diffraction and moves against the tilt; glare is reflection and follows it. Running both, opposed, is what gives the surface a material.
props.idleDrift: How much the foil keeps moving with no pointer on it, on two incommensurate rates so the idle never settles into an obvious period. A card in a case is never quite still, and a completely dead card in a grid reads as an image rather than an object.
props.settle: Seconds the card takes to catch up to the pointer. Near zero it is welded to the cursor and reads as a texture map; too high and it lags far enough that the foil stops feeling attached to your hand.
props.blendMode: How the foil composites onto whatever you wrapped. Colour-dodge behaves like real foil — it blows out where the card is already bright and does almost nothing in the shadows. Screen is the safe one on a light card.
props.sheenColor: The colour carried by the specular sheen.

lens.description: A glass lens you drag across live content, bending it through an SVG displacement field with a real bevel and three-channel dispersion. It refracts a live duplicate of its own children rather than the page backdrop, which is the only version of this effect that works in Chrome, Safari and Firefox alike.

props.size: Diameter of the disc, measured against the shorter side of whatever it is dropped into rather than in pixels — so the glass keeps its proportion in a wide hero and in a narrow column alike, and can never outgrow the box on either axis. The displacement map is rasterised once at a fixed resolution and stretched to fit, so dragging this is cheap; regenerating a bitmap per frame would cost far more than the pixels are worth.
props.refraction: How far the map pushes the content, and the one number this component is about. It runs through the filter property on a live duplicate rather than through backdrop-filter, because backdrop-filter with an SVG reference is Chromium-only — and CSS.supports reports true in WebKit and Gecko too, so the capability cannot even be detected honestly.
props.edgeThickness: How much of the radius is bevel. Real glass does nearly all of its bending in the last fifth, which is why displacing evenly across the whole disc gives a soap bubble rather than a lens.
props.blur: Softening behind the glass, and it ships at zero on purpose. Blur is the fastest way to make a lens look like a smudge — real glass is sharpest dead centre, so anything past about three stops being an optic and becomes a frosted coaster you cannot read through. At zero the blur is dropped from the filter list rather than written as blur(0px), which would still buy a render surface for no visible effect.
props.chromatic: Separation between the three channels' displacement — three real passes, isolated by colour matrices and recombined additively. Scaled by the disc rather than fixed in pixels, so the same setting is the same optic at any size. Glass disperses; a single pass with a tinted edge is a smear pretending to be physics.
props.magnify: Scale applied to the content inside the disc. It is a real transform rather than a displacement, because displacement can only resample pixels that are already there — faking magnification with it softens the entire window, which is exactly what makes most browser lenses read as a smear. Below one it is a fisheye pushed the wrong way: a real optic, and one that looks broken to everyone who is not an optician.
props.shimmer: Speed of the specular travelling the rim. It is the only thing here that moves on its own, and it is what stops a parked lens looking like a screenshot.
props.friction: How much of a throw survives, applied per second rather than per frame so the same flick coasts the same distance on a 60Hz and a 120Hz display.
props.bounded: Which box holds the lens in, and what it is looking at. On, it stays inside its container and magnifies a live duplicate of the children you handed it. Off, it is portalled to the body and bound to the viewport instead — dropping the container's own clip is not enough, because any ancestor that clips wins and on a real page there is always one — and what it magnifies becomes the whole page. Either boundary resists and reverses rather than stopping dead; a thrown object that halts against an invisible wall reads as a bug rather than as a boundary. The page is duplicated for real, because no browser API lets an element read arbitrary rendered content: backdrop-filter cannot magnify and is Chromium-only. That copy is a snapshot rather than a live tree, re-taken on every grab, so it cannot carry a running animation, canvas pixels or component state.
props.rimColor: The colour of the rim highlight, masked to the outermost two pixels so it reads as the lit edge of the glass instead of a ring drawn on top of it.

passcode.description: A one-time-code field whose cells answer every keystroke. Each character lands compressed and springs back, a paste distributes across the row rather than filling it on one frame, a wrong code shakes and clears itself, and a right one folds the whole row into a tick. Underneath there is exactly one real input holding the whole code, which is what keeps SMS autofill, password managers, select-all and a screen reader working. None of those survive six inputs with maxLength one.

props.length: Cells in the code. Six is the industry default because it is about the longest string most people can hold in working memory between reading it and typing it — the control exists so you can feel where that stops being true.
props.mode: What the field accepts. Numeric also asks for the number pad, which matters far more on a phone than the validation does — an alphanumeric code field that opens a full keyboard costs the user two taps every single time.
props.mask: Render dots instead of characters. Off by default on purpose: a one-time code is worthless a minute after it arrives, and masking it only stops the person entitled to read it from checking their own typing.
props.stiffness: Spring tension of the per-character pop. High enough to land inside the gap between two fast keystrokes, or the cells queue up behind a quick typist and the feedback arrives after the character it is confirming.
props.damping: Spring friction. Low rings past and settles, which is the difference between a cell that acknowledges a keystroke and one that merely updates.
props.anticipation: How far a cell compresses before it springs back. A brief gather in the opposite direction is what makes the pop read as the cell reacting rather than as the cell being resized — at zero it is a plain overshoot and noticeably flatter.
props.pasteStagger: Delay between cells as a pasted or autofilled code distributes. Zero fills every cell on one frame, which is honest and reads as a glitch; the stagger turns an instantaneous state change into something the eye can follow.
props.shakeAmplitude: Lateral travel of the rejection. It moves the whole row rather than the cells individually — a row that shakes has been judged, a set of cells that each shake looks broken.
props.autoSubmit: Judge the code the moment the last cell fills instead of waiting for a button. Correct when a wrong answer costs nothing; wrong the instant it does.
props.submitDelay: Pause between the last character landing and the verdict. It exists so the final cell finishes its own pop before the row is judged — validating on the same frame steals the confirmation of the keystroke that caused it, and the user never learns their last character registered.
props.accentColor: The focused cell's ring, the filled border, the caret, and the success tick.
props.errorColor: The rejection. It takes the cell borders rather than flooding the fills, so the code you typed stays readable while you are being told it is wrong.

dial.description: A machined rotary knob: angular drag with detents you can feel on the way past, inertia on a flick, and a spring that settles into the nearest stop. The angle lives in a motion value rather than in React state, because a drag writes it sixty times a second and a spring more often than that, so the only thing React holds is the detent index, and only when that integer actually changes. Arrow keys step through the same spring the hand does, so the keyboard is not a second, worse path to the same control.

props.detents: Stops across the sweep. This is the resolution of the control and it changes how the drag feels as much as how it reads: few stops far apart give a decisive click between settings, many close together give something closer to a continuous ramp with a texture.
props.sweep: Angular range, centred on twelve o'clock. Two hundred and seventy is the instrument convention because it leaves a visible gap at the bottom — the eye reads the gap as the end of the scale, so both limits are legible without a label. At a full turn there are no ends to see.
props.stiffness: How hard the spring pulls toward the chosen stop after release. High makes a knob that arrives the instant you let go; low makes one with weight, where a flick keeps travelling for a moment after the finger is gone.
props.damping: How much of that spring's energy is absorbed. Below about fifteen the knob overshoots its stop and comes back, which reads as a loose detent rather than a machined one.
props.inertia: How far a flick carries past the point the hand let go. The throw is projected first and the nearest stop chosen second, so a fast spin travels several detents and settles — at zero the knob stops at whichever stop it happened to be passing, which throws the whole gesture away.
props.detentPull: Magnetism felt during the drag itself, before any release. The pull falls off toward the midpoint between two stops, so the exact centre is an unstable point the knob slides off rather than a flat spot it can rest in — which is what makes a detent feel like a notch instead of a suggestion.
props.ticks: How the stops are marked on the panel around the knob. The scale never turns with the pointer — a mark that moves with the thing it is measuring tells you nothing about where you are.
props.readout: The value under the knob, set in tabular figures so the number does not shuffle sideways as it counts.
props.accent: The lit tick, the pointer line, and the live half of the readout.
props.size: Knob diameter. Everything inside is drawn against a fixed grid and scaled, so the knurling, the bevel and the pointer keep their proportions at any size.

refract.description: A frosted-glass slab you drag across a live scene, refracting it through a real shader optic. A rounded-rect height field bends three separately-sampled color channels along its gradient, with a Fresnel-bright rim, a travelling specular streak, and a frost that is a genuine multi-tap blur of what sits beneath the pane. Where Lens bends its DOM children through an SVG displacement map and magnifies, Refract is a flat pane over a scene texture with true angle-of-incidence refraction, dispersion and glare, and the scene it bends is drawn in the same shader, because no browser lets WebGL read the rendered page. Throw it and it glides on momentum, rubber-banding off the container walls.

props.ior: Refraction strength at the bevel. The flat middle passes almost straight through, exactly like a real pane.
props.dispersion: R/G/B sample spread — the chromatic fringe that gathers on the bevel.
props.edgeWidth: Fraction of the slab that is bevel — all of the bending and most of the glare lives there.
props.glare: Fresnel rim and travelling specular strength.
props.slabWidth: Slab width as a fraction of the container.
props.scene: The procedural backdrop being refracted. High-frequency scenes show the dispersion hardest.

lever.description: An industrial breaker lever with a real over-centre mechanism. Displayed travel lags the raw pointer travel by a bump curve peaked at the threshold, so approaching it the handle drags heavier, and crossing it the lag collapses and the handle races ahead of the finger. That is why a half-hearted push falls back the way a real breaker does. Release projects the flick's velocity past the threshold before choosing a side, so momentum can finish a throw the finger only started, and the keyboard commits through exactly the same spring the hand uses. The throw is a motion value. React holds only the committed side.

props.orientation: Throw axis. Vertical reads as a breaker; horizontal as a transfer switch.
props.stiffness: Spring tension on the snap.
props.damping: Spring friction — low enough by default to overshoot and settle.
props.resistance: The hump — how hard the mechanism fights before it commits.
props.labels: ON / OFF stencils on the housing.
props.accent: The lamp, the lit end of the track, and the handle stripe.
props.size: Housing height (width when horizontal); internals scale on a fixed grid.

tear.description: A ticket with a perforated stub you tear off for real. The ticket is drawn twice and cut from one seeded jag polygon: an attached layer holds everything still connected, the body plus the stub below the tear front, and a flap layer holds only the freed part, rotated about the frontmost attached point, so the torn edges mate tooth for tooth and the swing can never overlap the body. The seam fights back through a resistance curve, a failed tear springs shut, and a completed one lets the stub fall under gravity carrying the release velocity. The jag array comes from a seeded PRNG so the edge never boils between renders.

props.perforationAt: Where the seam sits across the ticket.
props.jag: Roughness of the torn edge — 0 is a die-cut, 1 is a bad day.
props.teeth: Perforation tooth count; also the resolution of the torn edge.
props.resistance: How hard the seam fights before it lets go.
props.gravity: How fast the freed stub falls away.
props.autoReset: Heal the ticket after the stub is gone.
props.inkColor: The ticket's printed ink — title, seat block, barcode.

grow-dialog.description: A dialog that grows out of the clicked element and shrinks back into it, entirely inside a portal — never behind page content.

props.stiffness: Spring stiffness of the grow.
props.damping: Spring damping — lower rings longer.
props.radius: Panel corner radius.
props.blurBackdrop: Frosted blur on the backdrop scrim.
props.autoFocus: Focus the first focusable element on open.

dismiss.description: Throw the top card away and the stack closes up behind it. Distance commits, but so does speed — a fast flick from barely anywhere counts, and anything short of both rubber-bands home carrying the velocity you let go at.

props.axis: Which way a card can leave. Sideways is the toast convention; downward reads as filing something away rather than discarding it.
props.threshold: How far across its own width a card must travel to commit. Distance is only half the test — a flick past the speed threshold commits from anywhere.
props.velocityThreshold: Release speed that commits regardless of how far the card actually moved. Without this a quick flick just springs back and the gesture feels deaf.
props.rubberBand: Give past the drag bounds. 0 is a hard wall; 1 follows the finger exactly and loses the sense that the card is resisting you.
props.stackDepth: How many cards are visible at once. Past four the ones at the back stop being legible and start being texture.
props.stackOffset: Vertical step between one card and the next down the stack.
props.stackScale: Scale lost per card down the stack. This is what sells depth — offset alone reads as a list.
props.rotateOnDrag: Degrees the card leans at the far edge of the throw. Derived from displacement, not animated separately, so an interrupted throw can never desync it.
props.stiffness: How hard the stack springs into its new slot after a card leaves.
props.damping: How fast that spring settles. Low values let the stack overshoot and bounce, which reads as lightweight.

flip-card.description: A grid card that flips out of its cell — GSAP Flip carries it to viewport center while it rotates to reveal its back face, then returns on close.

props.flipDuration: Duration of the Flip flight; rotation timing derives from it.
props.expandedWidth: Expanded card width (clamped to the viewport).
props.expandedHeight: Expanded card height (clamped to the viewport).
props.backdropBlur: Backdrop scrim blur while a card is open.

unfold.description: A row of slats that open on approach while their neighbours give up the room on a spring.

props.expandRatio: How much wider the open slat is than a closed one.
props.stiffness: Spring stiffness — higher snaps open faster.
props.damping: Spring damping — lower overshoots and settles.
props.labelReveal: Turn the vertical rail label horizontal on open.
props.useImage: Fade each panel's cut-out artwork in behind its slat.

focus-grid.description: A five-tile bento where any tile you pick takes the large slot and the rest slide back into order around it.

props.radius: Corner radius of each tile.
props.stiffness: Spring stiffness — higher lands faster.
props.damping: Spring damping — lower overshoots and settles.
props.captions: Show the small label on the supporting tiles.
props.heroSide: Which edge the large slot sits against.

intro-animation.description: A wind front sweeps the wordmark right to left. The instant it reaches a glyph the text hands off to a baseline-aligned field of GPU grain — same pixels, same colour, no seam — which peels crown-first and drifts away as smoke through a curl field. The backdrop opens behind it to reveal the page. Mount it over your app and unmount on onDone.

props.sweepDuration: Time the wind front takes to cross the wordmark. Everything downstream is derived from it — the reveal fires at 93.7% of the sweep, so shortening it tightens the whole sequence rather than leaving the plume stranded after a fast wipe.
props.grainDensity: Grains sampled per glyph. The sampling stride adapts to font size, so this is a count and not a spacing — a glyph holds roughly this many points whether it renders at 28px or 112px. The performance knob: every grain is one point in a single draw call, and changing it re-rasterizes the word.
props.windSpeed: How hard the wind carries released grains downstream. Each grain keeps its own speed rank, so the motion-blur ghosting on the fastest ones survives turning the wind down — the plume slows without flattening into a uniform sheet.
props.buoyancy: How fast the plume climbs. Lift also feeds the wind shear, so raising it does not just push the dust up — it rakes the risen grains further ahead and bends the plume into a curve instead of a diagonal.
props.turbulence: Amplitude of the divergence-free curl field the grains are advected through. The field is sampled at each grain's travelling position, so grains meet new eddies as they fly — that is the difference between smoke and shimmer. At zero the dust is pure ballistics.
props.grainSize: Size of an individual grain. The base covers the sampling stride so the held letter reads as solid ink; push it far below 1 and the handoff starts to show the lattice underneath.
props.splitIndex: How many characters carry the ink colour before the accent takes over. The tint travels with each grain, so the dust keeps the colour of the letter it came from all the way out.
props.reveal: How the backdrop leaves. Split slides two halves apart from the centre line; fade dissolves it in place; none draws no backdrop at all, so the wordmark erodes over whatever is already behind it.
props.autoplay: Replay the sequence on a loop. Off is the real thing: the intro plays once, calls onDone, and returns false to the loop host so it stops costing frames for good.
props.replayDelay: Pause between the plume clearing and the wordmark reassembling. Long enough to read as a fresh entrance rather than a stutter.
props.inkColor: Colour of the leading characters and the dust that comes off them.
props.accentColor: Amethyst on the characters from the split onward. A uniform, not baked into the grain buffer, so dragging it never re-rasterizes the word.
props.backgroundColor: The field the wordmark sits on and the thing the reveal opens. Its own material rather than a themed surface — an intro that flashes white in a light theme defeats the point of covering the page.

magnetic-dock.description: A dock whose items swell under the pointer and carry their neighbours part of the way with them. One shared value drives the whole row, so nothing re-renders while you sweep across it — and focusing an item writes the same value, which is why the keyboard gets the identical effect rather than a substitute for it.

props.magnification: How far the item directly under the pointer grows past its resting size. Past about 2.5 the peak stops looking like the row lifting and starts looking like one icon detaching from it.
props.falloff: Distance at which an item stops responding at all. This is the real character knob: a narrow falloff magnifies one item and reads as a hover state, while a wide one pulls four or five along and reads as a surface being pushed from underneath.
props.baseSize: Resting edge length of an item. The icon is sized in `em` off this, so any node scales with it without knowing the dock exists.
props.gap: Space between items at rest. Items grow into this gap rather than pushing each other along, so a tight dock has the peak crowding its neighbours and a loose one lets each swell finish.
props.stiffness: How hard an item springs toward its target size. Low values put the largest item visibly behind the pointer on a fast sweep, which breaks the illusion that you are pushing the surface yourself.
props.damping: How fast that spring settles. Under about 15 the icons keep bobbing after the pointer has left, which is charming once and irritating thereafter.
props.labels: Fade the item's label in over the magnified item. Its opacity is driven by the same distance the size is, so it arrives with the swell instead of on a separate hover timer.
props.orientation: Which axis the dock runs along, and therefore which pointer coordinate drives it. Items always grow away from the dock's own edge, so a vertical rail expands sideways rather than upward.
props.accent: Running indicator and focus ring. The ring is a shadow rather than an outline — an outline paints outside the border box and visibly lags the spring while the button is still resizing.

radial-menu.description: Press and hold anywhere and the options fan out from the point you pressed. Selection is resolved from the pointer's angle rather than by hit-testing the options, so every target is an infinite wedge — commit to a direction and you can throw the pointer as hard as you like and still land it.

props.radius: How far the options sit from the press point. Only the drawing distance — selection is angular, so a wide radius costs nothing in accuracy and a tight one buys none.
props.startAngle: Where the first option lands. 0 is right and 90 is down, following screen coordinates rather than the maths convention — the y axis on a page points the other way and pretending otherwise makes every later value read backwards.
props.sweep: Total arc the options are spread across. At a full turn the last option would land on the first, so the spacing switches from end-to-end to evenly-around at 360 — the one place this component has two layout rules.
props.itemCount: How many options to show. Past about seven the wedges get narrower than the flick they are meant to catch, which is the point at which a list would serve you better.
props.holdDelay: How long the press has to be held before the fan opens. Releasing sooner is treated as a plain click on whatever is underneath, so the surface stays usable for its normal purpose. At 0 the menu opens on contact and that normal purpose is gone.
props.stagger: Delay between one option arriving and the next. Small values read as the fan unrolling; large ones make you wait for the option you already know you want.
props.stiffness: How hard the options spring out to their positions.
props.damping: How fast that spring settles. Low values overshoot the arc and snap back, which reads as the options being flung rather than placed.
props.centerCancel: Radius of the dead zone around the press point. Release inside it and nothing commits. At 0 a press that never really moved still resolves to whichever option is nearest the jitter, and the menu picks something you never chose.
props.accent: Highlight on the option the pointer is aimed at, and on the label echoing it back at the centre.

live-activity.description: A live activity tracker in one black shape. A timer, a download, a delivery, a song and an AI agent take turns in it, and tapping it opens a full card. The text fades out before the shape moves and comes back after it stops, so it never stretches during the resize. The small pill and the big card share one clock and one state, so if you pause in the card, the pill is paused too. The agent is the main show. Three sparkles circle on a tilted orbit, the front one big and the back ones small, and they spin faster on every new step. The pill widens to show each new step's name, then shrinks back to the step count, and the card types out the command the agent is running.

props.activity: Which activity holds the island. Changing it morphs the shell straight to that activity's pill and switches the cycle off — a hand-picked activity that a timer replaces four seconds later was never really picked.
props.autoCycle: Rotate through the activities on a timer. The rotation stands still while the island is expanded, hovered or holding focus — nothing should change under a pointer that is about to tap it. Switching it off returns the island to `activity`, so the control and the island never disagree.
props.cycleInterval: How long each activity holds the island before the next takes over. Under about three seconds there is no time to read the number before it becomes a different one.
props.stiffness: How hard the shell springs toward its new size. The pill-to-card swell is the largest move the island makes, so this is what decides whether it reads as a drop or a crawl.
props.damping: How fast the spring settles. The default leaves one small overshoot, which is what sells the shape as liquid rather than a box being resized; under about 18 it wobbles on every activity swap.
props.contentBlur: Blur the content dissolves through on its way in and out. It hides the frames where the outgoing and incoming views overlap; at 0 the swap reads as a plain crossfade.
props.accent: Progress rings, the download bar, the agent's working state and the focus outline. The timer and delivery keep their own tints so you can tell the activities apart at a glance.

scratch.description: A scratch-off card. Drag over the foil to scrape it off, and small flakes fall where you scratch. Once enough foil is gone, the rest fades away on its own. A light glints across the foil now and then. You can also focus the card and press Enter or Space to reveal it.

props.threshold: How much foil has to come off before the rest falls away.
props.revealDuration: How long the leftover foil takes to fade out.
props.flakes: Foil flakes fall from where you scratch.
props.glint: A light sweeps across the foil now and then.
props.glintColor: The light that sweeps across the foil. The focus ring uses it too.
props.foilColor: The foil. Its flakes take their color from it.

swipe-actions.description: List rows you swipe to show actions, like in iOS Mail. Drag a row and its buttons slide in from the side. Swipe all the way and the outer action fills the row and runs. An action like Archive then folds the row away. A quick flick works too. With full swipe off, the row pushes back when you pull past the last button. With a keyboard, the arrow keys show the actions and Enter runs one.

props.revealWidth: Width of each action button once it is fully shown.
props.fullSwipe: Swipe far enough and the outer action fires on its own.
props.fullSwipeThreshold: How far across the row a full swipe has to go.
props.rubberBand: How much the row resists past the last button when full swipe is off. 0 is a hard stop. iOS uses 0.55.
props.velocityThreshold: A flick faster than this opens or closes the row, however short it is.
props.stiffness: How hard the row springs to where it lands.
props.damping: How fast that spring settles. Lower values bounce.

sheet.description: A bottom sheet with three heights: peek, half and full. Drag the header and let go. The sheet carries the speed of your hand forward and snaps to the height it was heading for, so a short flick from the bottom can reach the top. Pull it past either end and it stretches like a rubber band. Above peek the page behind dims and steps back. A pull or a flick past the bottom closes it. Arrow keys on the handle step between heights, and Escape closes.

props.peek: Height of the lowest stop, as a share of the container.
props.half: Height of the middle stop, as a share of the container.
props.stiffness: Spring tension of the snap. Higher lands sooner.
props.damping: Spring friction. Low values bounce at the stop before they settle.
props.rubberBand: How far the sheet gives when you pull it past its ends. 0 is a hard stop.
props.backdrop: How dark the page behind gets when the sheet is at full height.
props.recede: The page behind scales back a little as the sheet rises.
props.dismissible: A pull or a flick past the lowest stop closes the sheet. Off, the lowest stop is the floor.
props.accentColor: The focus ring on the handle.

command-palette.description: A cmdk command menu with a plain or liquid-glass surface and hotkey trigger.

props.hotkey: Shortcut that opens the palette. cmd+k falls back to Ctrl+K on non-Apple platforms.
props.loop: Wrap keyboard selection at the list ends.
props.glass: Liquid-glass surface instead of a solid panel.

physics-engine.description: A from-scratch 2D rigid-body physics lab. Fixed-timestep impulse solver, drag-to-throw bodies, force and velocity overlays, and a live energy readout on a blueprint grid.

props.scene: Preset world. Switching rebuilds the scene deterministically from a fixed seed.
props.gravity: Uniform downward gravity. 0 is zero-g — throw bodies and watch them coast.
props.restitution: Bounciness of every collision, applied live to existing bodies. Impacts below 1 m/s are absorbed so stacks can settle.
props.friction: Coulomb friction coefficient for all contacts, applied live. 0 is ice; boxes need around 0.3 to stack.
props.timeScale: Simulation speed. Physics always steps at a fixed 120 Hz — this scales how much simulated time each frame consumes. 0 freezes time.
props.bodyCount: How many bodies the playground rains and how tall the stack and wrecking-ball towers build. Projectile ignores it.
props.sizeVariation: Spread of playground body sizes — 0 rains uniform bodies, 1 mixes pebbles with boulders. Density is fixed, so bigger really is heavier.
props.showVectors: Velocity (green, solid) and net-force (red, dashed) arrows anchored at each body's center of mass, scaled to magnitude.
props.trails: Fading motion trails behind moving bodies — read parabolas and pendulum arcs at a glance.
props.showEnergy: Live HUD readout of kinetic, potential, and total energy in joules, computed from solver state every step — never faked.
props.tint: Accent color for dynamic bodies, trails, and the grab spring. Grid and chrome follow the theme.

black-hole.description: A real-time Schwarzschild black hole raytraced per-pixel in a WebGL2 shader. Null geodesics bend a lensed accretion disk over the event horizon, with Doppler beaming, gravitational redshift, a photon ring, and a lensed starfield, all under a cinematic orbit.

props.steps: Geodesic integration steps per ray. Higher sharpens the lensing and photon ring; lower runs faster. The single heaviest cost in the shader.
props.diskInner: Inner disk radius in Schwarzschild radii. 3 Rs is the ISCO — the innermost stable circular orbit around a non-spinning hole.
props.diskOuter: Outer edge of the accretion disk, in Schwarzschild radii.
props.diskBrightness: Overall emission of the accretion disk.
props.ringColor: Recolors the accretion disk. White keeps the physical blackbody gradient (gold → white → blue) and the Doppler asymmetry; pick a hue to tint the ring without dimming it.
props.dopplerMax: Relativistic Doppler beaming and redshift strength. 0 flattens the disk to symmetric; 1 is the physical approaching-side-brighter, receding-side-dimmer asymmetry.
props.starBrightness: Brightness of the gravitationally lensed background stars and Milky Way band.
props.skyFloor: Ambient deep-space glow filling the void behind the stars. Tinted by the halo color.
props.rotationSpeed: Speed of the cinematic camera orbit and the disk's differential swirl. 0 stops both.
props.fov: Observer camera field of view. Wider pushes the hole smaller and exaggerates the lensing curvature; narrower zooms in and flattens the perspective.
props.bloomStrength: Intensity of the HDR bloom that blooms the bright disk and photon ring. 0 disables the bloom passes entirely.
props.bloomRadius: Spread of the bloom blur. Disabled when bloom is 0.
props.grain: Animated fine film grain over the final image.
props.chromaticAberration: Lens-edge color fringing, strongest toward the corners.
props.autoOrbit: Spin the camera continuously left-to-right around the hole at a fixed distance. Drag to take manual 360° control; the orbit resumes a few seconds after you let go and keeps spinning around your current view — it never resets the angle. Off freezes the current view, which you can still drag.
props.debug: Diagnostic shader outputs — step-count heatmap, disk-hit mask, closest-approach radius, escape direction, and the redshift factor.
props.tint: Accent that tints only the outer halo, photon ring, sky floor, and hero-star glow. The accretion disk keeps its physical blackbody color.

vortex-bloom.description: A molten-gold-and-obsidian vortex funnel spiraling into a luminous SDF core, either lotus, gem, or flame, raymarched per-pixel in a WebGL2 shader, with a GPU dust field spiraling down the flow toward the throat, all under a draggable orbit and a real two-pass bloom.

props.primary: Molten-gold high tone — the color of the swirling streaks and the throat glints.
props.secondary: Obsidian deep tone — the funnel's shadowed lanes and the void behind it.
props.accent: Luminous core-emission tint. Drives the color of the convergence bloom and the dust as it reaches the core.
props.coreObject: The centerpiece sitting at the vortex's convergence — a layered petal lotus, a faceted crystal, or an animated flame plume. Swapping it never moves the point the dust flows toward.
props.coreScale: Scales the centerpiece — lotus, gem, or flame — up or down without moving the convergence the dust flows toward.
props.stemLength: Length of the lotus stalk hanging into the flow beneath the flower. Lotus only; 0 removes it.
props.vortexIntensity: Swirl speed, streak turbulence, and dust inflow speed. Higher winds the funnel tighter and faster.
props.glowIntensity: Core emission and HDR bloom strength. Drives how hard the convergence and the dust bloom.
props.particleDensity: Dust grains spiraling down the flow. Capped at 1200 to hold 60fps on a mid-range GPU.
props.particleSpeed: How fast the dust grains stream down the flow toward the core, independent of the swirl speed.
props.smokeAmount: Soft, low-frequency atmospheric haze drifting behind the ribbons. 0 leaves crisp streaks on obsidian; higher fills the frame with smoke.
props.cameraAutoRotate: Continuously orbit the funnel. Drag to take 360° control; the orbit resumes around your current view a moment after you let go.
props.rotationSpeed: Speed of the cinematic camera orbit.
props.fov: Observer field of view. Wider exaggerates the whirlpool's depth; narrower flattens it.
props.verticalOffset: Slides the whole vortex up or down in the frame without moving the camera — recenter the eye where you want it.
props.chromaticAberration: Lens-edge color fringing, strongest toward the corners.
props.grain: Animated fine film grain over the final image.

smoke-field.description: A real-time GPU fluid you can stir. Semi-Lagrangian advection, a Jacobi pressure solve, and vorticity confinement run every frame across ping-ponged float buffers, injecting a dark amethyst plume that curls, billows, and bleeds through the frame wherever you drag.

props.dyeColor: Color of the dye injected into the fluid.
props.quality: Bundles simulation and dye buffer resolution. Higher is finer and costlier.
props.pressureIterations: Jacobi pressure passes per frame — higher makes the flow tighter and more incompressible.
props.velocityFade: How long motion persists before it dissipates.
props.densityFade: How long the dye lingers before fading out.
props.curl: Vorticity-confinement strength — swirl detail. 0 skips the curl passes.
props.splatRadius: Size of the dye and force splat under the pointer.
props.splatForce: Velocity impulse imparted by a pointer drag.
props.autoPlume: Continuously inject a rising plume at the base when idle.
props.buoyancy: Upward force lifting the dye, so smoke rises. 0 lets it drift neutrally.
props.grain: Animated grain over the final image.

ripple-field.description: A pool of dark, moonlit water you disturb by hand. A leapfrog solve of the 2D wave equation runs on a ping-ponged float field, ringing every pointer move outward, reflecting the swell off the walls, and lighting the surface with gradient-normal refraction, curvature-focused caustics, and a Fresnel glint riding each wavefront.

props.waterColor: Amethyst tint of the water — specular glints, caustics, and crest light.
props.deepColor: Deep pool base color the surface sits over.
props.quality: Simulation grid resolution. Higher is crisper and costlier.
props.tension: Wave propagation speed. Higher spreads ripples faster; the leapfrog solve caps below 0.5 to stay stable.
props.damping: Per-step energy retention — toward 1 the ripples ring on longer.
props.splatForce: Displacement a pointer drag or ambient drop carves into the surface.
props.splatRadius: Size of the surface dimple under the pointer, in screen fractions.
props.refraction: How strongly the surface slope bends the pool floor beneath the ripples.
props.specular: Intensity of the specular and Fresnel glints on each wavefront.
props.glossiness: Specular tightness — higher is a sharper, glassier highlight.
props.caustics: Brightness of the caustic threads where converging wavefronts focus light.
props.autoRipple: Randomly drop into the pool when idle so it never sits perfectly still.
props.grain: Animated fine grain over the final image.

umbral-orrery.description: A planet, its moons and their sun, drawn by one ray-traced shader. Each moon casts a real eclipse shadow on the planet, dark in the middle and soft at the edge. A moon turns ember red when it passes into the planet's own shadow. Drag to move the camera around to the night side, where the atmosphere lights up as a ring.

props.moonCount: How many moons orbit the planet.
props.orbitSpeed: Speed of every orbit. Inner moons always go around faster than outer ones.
props.tilt: Turns the orbits around the line from the sun to the planet. Every moon still makes an eclipse at any tilt.
props.moonSize: Size of the moons. The planet's radius is 1.
props.sunSize: Size of the sun in the sky. A bigger sun gives softer shadow edges.
props.atmosphere: Strength of the glow around the planet.
props.trails: Brightness of the orbit lines. 0 hides them.
props.drift: How fast the camera circles on its own. 0 keeps it still.
props.sunColor: Color of the sun and its light.
props.planetColor: Main color of the planet's cloud bands.
props.backgroundColor: Color of space behind the scene.

parallax-rail.description: A pinned section where scrolling down drives content sideways across depth planes moving at different rates.

props.planes: How many depth planes to render.
props.travel: Multiplier on the front rail's travel across the pin.
props.depthSpread: How much slower the backmost plane moves than the front.
props.damping: Spring damping on the scrub — higher tracks scroll exactly.
props.fadeEdges: Width of the soft mask at each rail edge.

approval-flow.description: A step-by-step approval checklist for agent permissions. Radio and checkbox groups, an "Other…" escape hatch that grows a field in place, and per-step validation that blocks the commit. Answering a step sends the chosen option flying into a running record of what you have already decided, so the screen accumulates a decision trail instead of replacing itself.

props.layout: Where the record of decided steps sits. A rail parks it beside the live step on wide screens; inline stacks it above.
props.morphDuration: Step change, option reveal and the escape hatch growing open. The flight into the record is a spring and ignores this — stiffness and damping own that one.
props.stiffness: How hard the chosen option is pulled toward its slot in the record.
props.damping: How fast that flight settles. Low values let the label overshoot its slot before landing.
props.density: Row height, padding and glyph size throughout.
props.revealStagger: Delay added per option as a step's list arrives. 0 lands the whole group at once.
props.shakeIntensity: Travel of the shake when a step is rejected. 0 disables it — the message and the red border still fire, because a rejection with no signal at all is a dead end.
props.shakeCycles: Round trips in that shake. Each one decays, and the last always ends on centre.
props.showProgress: Completion bar and step count above the live step.
props.autoAdvance: Commit a single-choice step the moment it is answered. Never applies to the escape hatch, which needs a sentence first, and it is forced off under reduced motion.
props.accentColor: Selection, checked glyph, progress fill and the approve button.
props.dangerColor: Invalid row border and the rejection message.

diff-review.description: A review surface for a patch an agent has proposed. Accept or reject each hunk, fold long runs of unchanged lines away, and flip between unified and split. Switching views does not redraw the diff: every line is a shared element that flies from the stream into its column and back, so you never lose the line you were reading.

props.defaultView: Starting layout. One interleaved stream, or the old file beside the new one. The toolbar toggle overrides it live.
props.morphDuration: Hunk fold, verdict change and the first reveal of a line. The flight between views is a spring and ignores this — stiffness and damping own that one.
props.stiffness: How hard a line is pulled toward its slot in the other view.
props.damping: How fast that flight settles. Low values let a line overshoot its column before landing.
props.stagger: Delay added per line as a hunk first appears. Capped at twelve lines in, so expanding a long fold never leaves the last row waiting in plain sight.
props.density: Row height and type size throughout.
props.showLineNumbers: Old and new line numbers in the gutter. Split view shows one per side; unified shows the surviving number.
props.contextLines: Unchanged lines kept on the side of a run that faces a change. The rest fold behind an expander — except a fold that would hide a single line, which costs a row to save a row.
props.collapseDecided: Fold a hunk's body away once it has a verdict, leaving the header and an Undo. Off keeps every hunk open so you can re-read what you just ruled on.
props.addColor: Added lines, their gutter sign, and an accepted hunk's edge.
props.delColor: Removed lines, their gutter sign, and a rejected hunk's edge.
props.accentColor: Active view toggle, fold expanders, focus rings and the reviewed counter once every hunk has been ruled on.

ledger.description: A live activity log for a working agent. Consecutive events from the same source fold into one block instead of stacking as identical rows, the window holds a fixed number and lets the rest fall off the top, and the scroll stays pinned to the newest line only until you scroll away from it. After that it keeps running and tells you how far behind you are.

props.speed: Multiplier on the whole cadence — typing and the gaps between events together.
props.charsPerSecond: Typing rate before jitter. The full text of an event is in the accessibility tree from the moment it arrives, so only the eye waits for this.
props.entryGap: Pause between one event landing and the next starting.
props.jitter: Spread on the per-event rate, metronome to wildly uneven. A fast burst draws a longer breath after it, so the unevenness reads as work rather than as noise. Seeded, not random — the same run is reproducible every mount.
props.maxEntries: Events retained before the oldest falls off the top, under a fade that keeps the window reading as a view onto a longer log.
props.group: Fold consecutive same-source events into one block with a count. The block wears the worst severity in it, so a denial folded in among routine reads still shows red.
props.showTimestamps: Elapsed stream time beside each block. Measured from the component's own clock, never from the wall clock, so it is identical on every replay.
props.caret: Blinking block caret on the line currently being written.
props.loop: Wrap to the first event when the source list runs out. Off lets the stream halt itself once, and the header reads complete.
props.density: Row height and type size throughout.
props.accentColor: Live indicator, caret, catch-up pill and the ok severity.

rotunda.description: Real HTML panels on a drag-spun 3D cylinder. A hand-rolled perspective projection written onto DOM elements rather than a canvas, so the text stays selectable, the links stay clickable, and a screen reader still reads every panel while the ring turns.

props.radius: Distance from the axis to each panel face. Together with the number of panels this decides whether the ring closes: too small for the count and the faces intersect, which is the one way this arrangement can look broken rather than tight.
props.perspective: Depth of the projection, and the control that decides whether this reads as expensive or as a cheap paper fan. Near enough and the front panel distorts violently; far enough and the ring flattens into a row of cards.
props.autoSpin: Idle rotation while nothing is being dragged. It stops the instant the pointer arrives and does not restart until it leaves, because a carousel that keeps moving under your cursor is a carousel you cannot read.
props.friction: How much of a fling survives, and the whole feel of the throw. Applied per second rather than per frame, so the same gesture coasts the same distance on a 60Hz and a 120Hz display — the naive per-frame form silently halves the throw on better hardware.
props.snap: Settle to the nearest panel once a fling drops below walking pace. Off, the ring stops wherever it stops — honest for a texture, wrong for a menu.
props.snapStiffness: How hard the ring is pulled to the nearest face. Damping is derived from it at the critical ratio, so raising this arrives faster without ever adding the overshoot that would read as a wobble on a menu.
props.depthDim: How far the back of the ring dims toward the background. Depth cueing sells the illusion harder than the rotation does, because a CSS transform gives you no occlusion to work with.
props.depthBlur: Blur on panels past the halfway point. Applied to an inner wrapper rather than the panel itself: a filter on a child of a preserve-3d parent establishes a containing block and flattens the entire ring into a stack.
props.faceCamera: Keep every panel square to the viewer rather than tangent to the ring. This turns the carousel into a card rack, and it is the right choice the moment the panels carry real copy you expect anyone to read off-centre.
props.dragSensitivity: Degrees of rotation per pixel of drag. The honest test is whether the panel under your finger stays under your finger — too low and the ring feels geared down, too high and a small gesture spins it past the panel you were reaching for.

ascii-engine.description: A lit, raymarched 3D solid rendered at exactly one pixel per character cell, then quantised into a glyph ramp drawn once with fillText. Drag to orbit it through a full three-sixty. Real geometry underneath, terminal on top, with no scene graph, no mesh, and no second library to get there.

props.solid: Which distance field is raymarched into the first pass. A field rather than a mesh: the silhouette stays exact at any cell size because it is evaluated instead of rasterised, which is why this needs no scene graph and no geometry upload.
props.charset: The glyph ramp, darkest to lightest. The atlas is drawn once with fillText into an offscreen canvas and uploaded as a single texture, so the shader just indexes it and a longer ramp costs nothing per frame.
props.cellSize: Width of one character cell, and the real resolution control. The first pass renders at exactly one texel per cell, so halving this quadruples the raymarch and changes nothing else — which makes it the honest performance dial rather than a cosmetic one.
props.spinSpeed: Rotation speed of the solid. At zero it parks, which is the only way to judge whether the ramp is actually resolving the form or just flickering convincingly.
props.tilt: Resting camera elevation. Dragging orbits from here rather than replacing it, so this control still means something after you have spun the solid around — and the pitch is clamped short of the poles, because a camera that rolls over the top reads as a bug rather than as a rotation you asked for.
props.zoom: How much of the frame the solid fills. It narrows the field of view rather than moving the camera in — dollying would clip the near face of the solid long before its silhouette filled the frame, which looks like a broken near plane rather than a close-up.
props.contrast: Gamma on the luminance before it picks a glyph, and what decides whether the solid reads as a form or as noise. The ramp has ten steps at most and the lighting has to spread across all of them — too little and the shape collapses into two characters.
props.edgeBoost: How much of the silhouette is added back before quantising. Pure luminance loses the outline — a ten-step ramp cannot carry both the shading and the contour, so without this the form dissolves into its own gradient.
props.glow: Bloom bleeding off the lit glyphs, driven by the cell's luminance rather than by the glyph's own coverage — so a bright cell glows whether it landed on a full block or a full stop.
props.inkColor: The phosphor the glyphs are printed in.

swarm.description: Up to a quarter of a million particles integrated entirely on the GPU, morphing between words and solids, with a drag-orbit camera. Position and velocity live in floating-point textures and never come back to the CPU. Text targets are sampled once out of an offscreen canvas, so the shape can be any string with no font atlas.

props.density: Particle count, as discrete steps rather than a slider. Each value reallocates four floating-point targets and rebuilds the geometry, and a slider would do that on every pixel of a drag. Sixty-five thousand is where letterforms close up. The simulation is nearly free above that — the cost is all fill rate — so the top step is for a machine you already know the answer about.
props.shape: What the cloud is heading for. Auto walks every form in turn — text, sphere, torus, grid — before repeating, and advances the word list one entry each time it comes back around to text; the rest hold. Disperse is the exception auto never lands on: its targets are uniformly random, so it is a state to send the cloud into rather than a form to morph between. Targets are sampled out of an offscreen 2D canvas, so the text form is whatever string you pass — the GPU never sees a glyph, only a texture of positions.
props.swapDuration: How long a shape holds before auto moves to the next one. This is the hold, not the travel — the morph itself is paced by morphSpeed, so a short duration with a slow morph gives a cloud that never quite arrives anywhere, which is a look rather than a mistake.
props.morphSpeed: How hard each particle is pulled toward its target. This is an acceleration, not a duration — the cloud arrives when the pull and the damping agree, which is why it never snaps. It also has to win against the turbulence: too low against a high curl and the letterforms never resolve, they just hover.
props.stagger: How much of the morph is spread across the cloud instead of happening at once. At zero every particle leaves and arrives together and it reads as a slide; near one the shape assembles over time and you can watch it build. The phase comes from each particle's own texel, so it does not reshuffle between shapes.
props.curl: Curl-noise turbulence applied on the way. Curl of a vector field is divergence-free by construction, so it stirs the cloud without ever thinning it or piling it up — which is the entire reason to use curl noise rather than plain noise on a velocity field, where the cloud slowly develops holes.
props.damping: How much velocity survives each step, applied per second rather than per frame. Below about 0.8 particles arrive dead and the shape has no life in it; above 0.97 they orbit their targets forever and never settle.
props.repel: How hard the pointer pushes particles away on hover. Dragging orbits the camera instead — sharing one gesture between the two would mean every attempt to look around also blew a hole in what you were looking at. The falloff is exponential in squared distance, so the hole has a soft edge and the cloud closes behind your cursor rather than leaving a permanent scar.
props.pointSize: Point sprite width, and the real performance control. Doubling it costs four times the shading at any density — at a quarter of a million particles the simulation is trivial and the fill rate is what falls over, which is the opposite of where most people expect the cost to be.
props.zoom: How close the camera sits to the cloud. Sprite size scales with it: leaving the points fixed makes a zoomed-in cloud read as sparser rather than nearer, which is the tell that a zoom is really a viewport crop.
props.autoSpin: Idle rotation while nothing is being dragged. Off holds the cloud still and hands the camera entirely to the pointer — a flung orbit still coasts to rest, since that motion was asked for. The drift exists to show the form is solid rather than a flat sprite, so turning it off is a choice about a still image, not a performance one.
props.particleColor: The colour of a settled particle.
props.accentColor: The colour of a moving one. Particles are blended between the two by their own speed, so the palette is a readout of the simulation rather than decoration laid over it.
props.backgroundColor: The void behind the cloud. Points blend additively, so this wants to stay genuinely dark — anything lighter and the dense core clips to white before the count is visible.

mirage.description: Live, fully interactive HTML seen through moving air. An animated turbulence field displaces the real DOM subtree per pixel, with no snapshot and no canvas replica, so the text stays selectable, the button still takes focus and the link is still a link while the whole panel shimmers.

props.mode: How the air moves. The four differ by the anisotropy of the noise rather than by strength: equal frequencies on both axes give soup, and a strongly biased axis is what makes a tear read as a tear instead of as more haze.
props.intensity: How far the content is pushed. This is genuine per-pixel displacement rather than a transform — a transform can only move the whole box, which is why skew-based heat haze never convinces. Past about one the text stops being readable, which is a legitimate look and a terrible default.
props.speed: Rate the field drifts. The noise is rasterised once as a seamless tile and scrolled, never re-seeded — stepping a turbulence seed swaps in an entirely unrelated field each time, which reads as a component tearing itself apart rather than as air moving. The wrap at one tile is invisible because the tile is seamless.
props.scale: Size of the turbulence cells, measured against a scrolling tile rather than against the element — so the same setting is the same air whether the panel is a card or a page. This sizes the tile itself, because a tile can hold no feature larger than its own period and the noise lattice only wraps on a whole number of cells; free the cell count instead and the field stops tiling, which shows up as the whole panel jumping to a different distortion once a wrap. Small cells shred the glyphs and large ones move the whole block as a unit; the interesting band is where a cell is roughly the height of a line of text.
props.chroma: Strength of the colour cast the shimmer carries, gathered where the pointer is. Hot air refracts, so a little colour separation is the cue that sells it as air rather than as a wobbling image.
props.trigger: What turns the effect on. Whichever you pick it eases rather than switches — a displacement that snaps on reads as the element being swapped out, one that rises reads as air beginning to move.
props.edgeHold: How much of the element's own silhouette is protected. Displacing evenly moves the border too, so a rounded card dissolves into an amoeba and the one edge a reader uses to locate it is the first thing destroyed. This tapers the push toward neutral near the boundary — at zero the outline shreds, and past about half the shimmer is confined to the middle of the panel.

submerge.description: Live content held under water. A slow current bends it continuously, a press drops a stone and a drag leaves a wake that trails behind the cursor. The text underneath stays selectable, the button still answers and the link is still a link, because the water bends the real tree rather than a picture of it.

props.depth: How deep the content sits. It drives the colour wash and adds to the bend, because the further under a surface something lies the further the same slope carries the light across it. Past about 0.8 the water starts winning and the content stops being the subject.
props.flow: Speed of the ambient current. The field is rasterised once as a seamless tile and scrolled rather than regenerated — regenerating costs a PNG encode per frame, which is why so many browser water effects settle for a static distortion instead.
props.turbulence: How hard the current bends the content. This is genuine per-pixel displacement of the live tree, not a transform — a transform can only move the whole box, which is the reason skewed 'underwater' text never convinces.
props.rippleForce: Strength of the disturbance the pointer leaves. A press radiates an isotropic ring; a drag leaves a wake — the same wave packet stretched along travel and weighted to the rear, so the water is disturbed where the pointer has been rather than around where it is. Sources are spaced by distance travelled rather than by pointer event, so the same gesture leaves the same wake at 60Hz or 120Hz.
props.rippleSpread: How far a disturbance travels before it dies. Growth is an exponential approach rather than a square root: both decelerate, but a square root has infinite slope at zero, so every ring is born already moving and the birth itself snaps. A drag wake spreads slower than a press ring, because a trail lingers where it was left.
props.settle: Seconds a disturbance takes to die away. Twelve run at once and a thirteenth reuses the oldest slot, so a fast drag always shows its newest wake rather than queueing behind stale ones — and twelve is enough that eviction rarely cuts one off mid-life, which is the pop that reads as jumpy.
props.edgeHold: How much of the element's own silhouette is protected. Displacing evenly moves the border too, so a rounded card dissolves into an amoeba and the one edge a reader uses to locate it is the first thing destroyed. At zero the outline shreds; past about half the water is confined to the middle.
props.waterColor: Shallow water — the colour every ring crest carries.
props.deepColor: Deep water. Applied as a multiply rather than an overlay, so the content keeps its own contrast instead of flattening behind a sheet of colour.

weave.description: A sheet of cloth on a position-based solver. Particles and distance constraints relaxed to convergence every fixed step, with no forces, no rotations and no contacts. Drag it, load it, and pull until the constraints fail and the tear runs. Every quad is shaded by its own extension against the tear threshold, so the load path through the sheet is visible long before anything breaks.

props.cols: Particles across the sheet. Constraint count grows as roughly twice cols times rows and every one is visited on every relaxation pass, so this and rows together are the honest cost dial.
props.rows: Particles down the sheet. Taller than it is wide is what makes the drape read as fabric; a square grid hangs like a banner and never folds.
props.iterations: Relaxation passes over the constraint list per fixed step. Position-based dynamics has no exact solve — it converges, and this is how far it gets. One pass is rubber, six is linen, and past ten you are paying for a stiffness you cannot see.
props.gravity: Uniform downward acceleration. Zero leaves the sheet floating so wind alone drives it, which is the clearest way to watch a strain wave cross the mesh.
props.wind: Lateral forcing, applied with a travelling phase rather than uniformly — a uniform push only translates the sheet and never ripples it.
props.stiffness: Fraction of each constraint's length error corrected per pass. One with enough passes is inextensible canvas; low values are jersey that stretches under its own weight. It trades against iterations almost multiplicatively — halving one and doubling the other lands in nearly the same place.
props.damping: Velocity bled off per step. Verlet carries velocity implicitly in the gap between the current and previous position, so this scales that gap rather than a stored vector — which is why it reads as air resistance and not as friction.
props.tearThreshold: Extension at which a constraint fails, as a multiple of its rest length. Evaluated after all relaxation passes, never during them: strain measured mid-solve is an artefact of the sweep order, and tearing on it produces failures that follow the constraint list rather than the load. Above about four nothing tears at any wind you can set.
props.pinMode: Which particles are held. Corners is the one worth pulling on — the load concentrates into two diagonals you can see in the strain field long before anything tears. Free drops the whole sheet, and is the honest demonstration that none of this is keyframed.
props.shading: How each quad is filled. Strain shades it by the extension of its own four edges, which is the point of the component: the load path through a hanging sheet is invisible in a wireframe and obvious the moment it is coloured.
props.tint: The cloth at rest — zero strain. Also the anchors and the ring on a held particle.
props.strainColor: The far end of the strain ramp, reached exactly at the tear threshold — so a quad going fully hot is a prediction rather than a decoration.

telemetry.description: A metric board that behaves as one instrument instead of eight sparklines. Hovering any tile broadcasts a single timestamp and every other tile resolves its own value at that same instant, so a latency spike and a queue backing up are visibly the same event rather than two coincidences. Threshold breaches are recorded on the sample rather than on a pixel, so the scar travels with its data and is still there forty seconds after the value recovered.

props.tiles: Metrics on the board. Every tile shares one clock and one cursor, so this is also how many traces a single hover has to answer at once — the coordination is the component, and it only becomes legible above about six.
props.columns: Grid width. Narrow columns make each trace taller relative to its width and exaggerate every wobble; wide ones flatten them into something you can actually compare across rows.
props.sampleRate: How often each ring buffer takes a sample, held independent of the frame rate on purpose. The buffer advances on its own accumulator, so a machine dropping to 30fps shows the same history as one at 120 — a chart whose past depends on the viewer's GPU is lying about the data.
props.history: How much past each trace shows. Ring capacity is this times the sample rate and is allocated once, so raising either reallocates rather than grows and the memory stays bounded.
props.smoothing: Exponential moving average applied on the way into the buffer. It smooths the stored series rather than the drawing, so the cursor reads exactly the numbers you can see — a readout that disagrees with its own trace is worse than a noisy one.
props.threshold: Normalised level a metric has to cross to count as a breach. Normalised because the tiles do not share units — a percentage and a megabyte have to be comparable for one cursor and one rule to mean anything across the board.
props.scars: Keep a permanent mark on the trace where a breach happened. A flash you missed is a flash that did not happen; the scar is what makes an unattended board worth glancing at.
props.cursor: The shared time cursor. Turning it off leaves eight ordinary sparklines, which is the clearest way to see what it was doing.
props.fill: Area under the trace. Gradient reads as volume without competing with the line; solid is denser and better at small tile sizes; none is the honest choice when several traces would otherwise imply a stack that does not exist.
props.traceColor: The line, the fill ramp, and the cursor rule.
props.breachColor: The threshold rule, the scar, and the readout while the cursor sits on a breached sample. One colour across all three, so a scar is visibly the same event as the reading that produced it.

rewind.description: An undo history you can scrub, and that refuses to throw the future away. Drag the head and the interface reverts live under your finger rather than on release. Act from a past point and the abandoned future stays drawn on the rail as a branch you can walk back onto, instead of being silently destroyed the way every real undo stack destroys it. Controlled in the same shape as Ledger: it owns the rail, the gesture and the branch graph, and your reducer owns the states.

props.orientation: Which axis the rail runs on. Horizontal reads as a scrubber; vertical reads as a commit log and stacks better beside a form. The gesture is written against one axis abstraction rather than two handlers, so the modes cannot drift apart.
props.scrubSnap: Lock the head to the nearest recorded state while dragging. Off, it moves continuously and the surface shows the state at or before it, which makes the density of the history visible — you can feel where you were working fast.
props.branching: Draw the futures you abandoned instead of discarding them. Off is the familiar destructive undo; on is the honest model, and the difference between the two is the whole component.
props.branchDepth: How many abandoned branches stay drawn beside the trunk before the oldest is folded away. Past about four the rail stops being a timeline and becomes a graph, which is a different component.
props.stiffness: Spring tension on the head. The marker and the reported index come off the same drag, so the surface can never show a state the head has not reached — a readout running ahead of its own scrubber is the single thing that makes time travel feel fake.
